title: Strong Refining Will Drive Chevron, ExxonMobil Q3 Results: Analyst - TradingView
content: TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman on Monday raised price forecasts for Chevron Corporation CVX and ExxonMobil Holdings XOM. Chevron: Analyst maintained a Hold rating and increased the price forecast from $205 to $215. The analyst writes that Chevron has outperformed the quarter to date following its Venezuela expansion announcement, with the asset expected to be equity accounted going forward. Gabelman estimates it could generate about $1 billion in free cash flow once production reaches 600,000 boe/d. The analyst expects Chevron to beat third-quarter estimates despite a $1.50-per-share timing headwind. Read Also:  Dozens Of U.S. Oil Refining And Business Groups Urge Trump To Reject Any Effort To Impose Ban On Diesel Exports Attention is also expected to remain on total cost of ownership (TCO), amid reports that a contract extension could require a large one-time payment and additional project equity, adds the analyst. Gabelman also expects an update on Kilby following a permitting pause in Texas and progress on additional projects, but does not expect Chevron to increase its buyback this quarter. The analyst estimates Upstream earnings to decline $1.2 billion quarter over quarter, or remain flat excluding timing headwinds. Lower commodity prices and Guyana shifting to profit oil are expected to reduce earnings by $0.2 billion each, offset by higher production excluding Guyana and TCO, plus lower TCO withholding taxes, adds the analyst. Downstream earnings are expected to fall $1.2 billion quarter over quarter, or rise $0.5 billion excluding timing impacts. Higher refining margins are estimated to add about $1 billion, partly offset by $0.2 billion from lower chemicals earnings and $0.4 billion from the removal of estimated second-quarter trading benefits. ExxonMobil: Analyst maintained a Buy rating and boosted the price forecast from $168 to $180. Exxon Mobil has underperformed during the Middle East conflict due to its outsized exposure to disrupted volumes, writes the analyst. Gabelman expects third-quarter results to beat consensus, supported by strong refining performance, while cash flow is also expected to exceed estimates despite a $2 billion timing headwind. The analyst said he is watching for signs that Exxon may accelerate Permian production growth following a series of midstream agreements, including its deal with Targa Resources. Attention will also focus on updates on Qatari LNG repairs and whether management remains comfortable with its concentrated LNG portfolio, adds the analyst. The analyst estimates upstream earnings to decline $0.6 billion quarter over quarter in the third quarter, with commodity prices and production each contributing $0.3 billion of pressure. The production impact is mainly due to Guyana shifting from cost to profit oil, while the commodity estimate includes a $0.4 billion benefit from normalized U.S. gas realizations. Energy Products earnings are estimated to increase $4.6 billion, driven mainly by higher margins, along with $0.3 billion from lower maintenance and $0.2 billion from lower costs. Chemicals earnings are expected to decline $0.5 billion and Specialty earnings $0.1 billion due to weaker margins. Price Action: Chevron shares were up 1.07% at $206.64 and ExxonMobil Holdings shares were up 1.03% at $162.25 at the time of publication on Monday, according to Benzinga Pro data. NYSE Composite moved back into the spotlight this week as firmer crude tied to Middle East and Iran-related tensions around the Strait of Hormuz lifted energy names, while the company detailed a multi-billion-dollar commitment in Venezuela aimed at expanding crude production over the coming years. The headline development for Chevron centers on a sizable multi-year commitment in Venezuela intended to raise the company's crude output there. The move arrived shortly after the United States advanced a broader oil arrangement with the country, reshaping the operating landscape for Western majors active in the region. For Chevron, deepening its Venezuelan footprint reflects a bet on barrels from a nation home to some of the largest crude reserves in the world. Expanding production in Venezuela carries distinctive operational and geopolitical considerations. The country's oil infrastructure has faced years of underinvestment, and lifting output requires capital, technical expertise, and a stable operating framework. Chevron's decision to press ahead signals confidence in the barrels it can bring online, even as the broader environment remains sensitive to regulatory shifts and sanctions dynamics that have shaped the region for years. Firmer crude has been a defining feature of recent sessions, with benchmark oil climbing amid concerns over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and wider Middle East friction. Brent crude reached elevated levels during September, and energy equities responded in kind. Chevron, as one of the largest integrated majors, tends to trade closely with crude sentiment given the weight of its upstream operations. For an integrated company, higher crude generally strengthens the cash-generating power of production while adding cost pressure to refining. Chevron's balance across upstream and downstream means the net effect depends on the interplay between the two, though periods of firm crude typically favor the upstream-heavy earnings mix that characterizes the company. The recent rally reinforced that pattern, keeping Chevron near the front of energy-sector discussion. Chevron shares reached an all-time high during September as Brent crude firmed on Hormuz-related shipping disruption. The stock has advanced meaningfully across the year, tracking the broader recovery in energy sentiment. Research desks responded by revising their price expectations, with at least one firm lifting its price objective substantially and another maintaining a constructive stance on the name. Such revisions typically follow updated crude assumptions and reassessments of a company's earnings power. For Chevron, the combination of firmer oil, the Venezuela commitment, and steady cost discipline featured prominently in how market participants framed the stock. Price expectation changes represent estimates rather than guarantees, but they illustrate the direction of sentiment across research coverage during an active stretch for the sector. Chevron paid a quarterly dividend during September and carries a multi-decade record of consistent dividend growth, a feature frequently highlighted when the market weighs large-cap energy names. Consistent distributions are a hallmark of the integrated majors, reflecting their scale and cash-generating capacity across commodity cycles. Chevron's long streak of annual dividend increases places it among a select group of companies known for steady cash distributions. Firmer crude tends to bolster the cash generation that underpins these distributions. When upstream barrels command higher prices, the resulting cash flow supports dividends alongside capital spending and balance-sheet management. Chevron's emphasis on maintaining and growing its payout has been a recurring theme in how the company communicates its financial priorities to the market. Chevron operates across the full hydrocarbon chain. Its upstream segment explores for and produces crude oil and natural gas across multiple regions, including significant activity in the Permian Basin of the United States, offshore developments, and international projects. Downstream, the company refines crude into fuels and lubricants and markets products through an extensive network, while a chemicals joint venture adds further diversification. The Permian Basin remains central to Chevron's domestic production, where the company has emphasized capital efficiency and steady volume growth. Alongside onshore shale activity, Chevron develops offshore and international resources that contribute barrels with varied cost and production characteristics. This diversified upstream mix is designed to provide resilience across different price environments and geographies. Chevron has outlined a capital spending framework that emphasizes disciplined allocation across its portfolio. After earlier industry cycles marked by heavy outlays, the major energy companies broadly shifted toward prioritizing cash generation and capital distributions over volume growth at any cost. Chevron has aligned with that approach, directing spending toward high-return projects while keeping overall budgets within a defined range. Capital discipline has become a defining feature of how the sector operates. By constraining spending and focusing on efficiency, integrated majors aim to sustain distributions and manage balance sheets through commodity swings. The company remains one of the most closely watched constituents within the wider universe of oil and gas stocks, where crude sensitivity, capital discipline, and dividend consistency frequently shape how the group is assessed. For market observers, the mix of macro forces and company-specific steps offers a window into how large energy firms adapt to a shifting backdrop. Whether through selective growth commitments abroad or disciplined capital allocation at home, Chevron continues to adjust its footprint in step with evolving demand and price dynamics, keeping the name firmly within the frame of sector-wide discussion during an active stretch for oil and gas. title: Chevron Is Expanding Its Presence in the Mediterranean. Here's What It Means for CVX Stock. - fool.com
content: Chevron will begin to explore for hydrocarbon deposits in Greek waters later this year. Last month, I wrote about how Chevron (CVX +0.94%) is well-positioned to benefit from the U.S. deal with Venezuela to develop some 65 billion barrels of that country's enormous proven oil reserves. But there's another region Chevron is moving into, which I think will also eventually help the stock. This week brought preliminary reports that the Houston-based oil and gas giant plans to begin seismic research in waters off Greece later this year, expanding its offshore exploration footprint in the Eastern Mediterranean. The news came from Greek Environment and Energy Minister Stavros Papastavrou, who was in the U.S. to attend United Nations meetings. The official met with a Chevron executive and agreed that the exploration could begin this year. A seismic exploration is the initial step in assessing hydrocarbon potential and must be conducted before any test drilling can begin. Earlier this year, Chevron was awarded four offshore leases to explore for oil around Greece. The oil giant already has assets in the Mediterranean, including two gas-producing fields off Israel and one in Cyprus. It also operates two exploration blocks in Egypt, with an agreement to explore for oil in Libya. Of course, oil stocks have gyrated this year with crude prices, which have moved in response to developments in the war in the Persian Gulf. But this month, Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told a conference that various mechanisms capable of moderating oil prices -- including strategic reserves and commercial inventories among them -- are now largely spent. He suggested that even a quick and unexpected end to the conflict with Iran wouldn't likely bring prices down softly or quickly. In addition, even when oil prices settle back to pre-war levels, a global shortage of refining capacity will remain. That, too, is a big plus for Chevron, with its spare capacity. For a retirement-focused investor looking at oil majors today, the choice comes down to Chevron (NYSE:CVX | CVX Price Prediction) versus ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), and the question is simple: Which one deserves the closer look right now for durable oil-patch income? Both are Dividend Aristocrats. Both are throwing off record cash. The differences matter for a retiree who needs the check to keep arriving through the next commodity cycle. Chevron pays more today. At $206.24 a share on Sept. 25, Chevron yields 3.45% on a $1.78 quarterly payout, with an annualized forward dividend of $7.12. Exxon, at $161.67, yields 2.55% on a $1.03 quarterly check and $4.12 annualized. Exxon owns the longer raise record: 43 consecutive years of annual dividend growth versus Chevron’s 39 consecutive annual increases. Both hiked roughly 4% in their latest raises, which puts both firmly in the Dividend Kings conversation (we ranked ten of them by valuation in a free report here). If your priority is the fattest current yield, Chevron wins this round. If your priority is the longest unbroken chain of raises through oil busts, Exxon wins. For a retiree writing checks in 2026, the higher cash yield today edges it: Chevron takes the income round. Chevron trades at a P/E of 32, a P/B of 2.13, and a P/FCF of 24. Exxon trades at a P/E of 23, a P/B of 2.52, and a P/FCF of 28. Exxon’s earnings yield of 4.42% comfortably beats Chevron’s 3.10%, and Exxon posts a higher ROE of 11.03% against Chevron’s 7.26%. Chevron has run harder recently, up 38.84% year to date versus Exxon’s 36.72%, and now trades at a richer multiple as it digests the Hess deal. On the numbers that decide what a retiree is paying per dollar of earnings, Exxon wins valuation. Dividend durability sits in the balance sheet, and the gap here is wide. Exxon carries a debt/equity of 0.17, net debt/EBITDA of 0.55, and interest coverage of 56.3x. Chevron’s figures: debt/equity 0.25, net debt/EBITDA 1.08, and interest coverage 13.7x. Chevron did cut $8.41 billion in total debt in Q2 2026, and management flagged net debt to CFFO of 0.6 times. Exxon’s is simply stronger. Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. Exxon hit record full-year production of 4.7 million oil-equivalent barrels per day, the highest in more than 40 years, with Guyana at roughly 900,000 barrels per day and a fifth FPSO on track for startup by year end. CFO Neil Hansen called Guyana “very much an inflection into free cash flow” and guided to “two times the level of free cash flow in 2030 than we saw in 2025.” Chevron’s record 4,070 MBOED is impressive, but it was driven by the Hess acquisition, which lifted leverage and DD&A. Exxon wins on durability. Exxon Mobil fits the income-focused retiree profile. You get a lower P/E, a fortress balance sheet, a longer 43-year raise record, and a Guyana ramp that materially raises the odds that the dividend keeps growing through the next down cycle. The starting yield is lower, but the check is more likely to be there in 2035. Chevron suits a different profile: the retiree who explicitly wants the highest current yield in the pair and is willing to accept a richer multiple and higher leverage after the Hess deal. If you need 3.45% today and trust management’s 2030 targets of 2% to 3% production growth and greater than 10% adjusted free cash flow growth, Chevron is defensible. title: Five Energy Stocks Set To Profit As Iran War Drags On (NYSE: CVX, NYSE: COP, NYSE: SHEL, NYSE: LNG, NYSE: MPC) - foreignpolicyjournal.com
content: By Ewan Scott | Sep 26, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis A prolonged conflict with Iran is opening multiple profit channels across the energy sector, from elevated crude prices to record refining margins, LNG shortages, and extreme shipping costs. Chevron (NYSE: CVX) is among the companies positioned to benefit from sustained higher oil and gas prices as Middle East tensions continue to disrupt global supply chains. ConocoPhillips (NYSE: COP) also offers investors meaningful exposure to elevated commodity prices, though its direct footprint in the Middle East differs from other majors, affecting the degree of disruption risk it carries. Shell (NYSE: SHEL) rounds out the trio of major integrated oil companies seen as well-placed to capitalize on the geopolitical premium now baked into global crude benchmarks. The level of direct Middle East exposure varies considerably across these three producers, meaning the risk profile and upside potential for each company differs in important ways for investors to weigh. Cheniere Energy (NYSE: LNG) stands out as a more direct beneficiary of the supply crunch, given its dominant position in the American liquefied natural gas export market, which has seen demand surge as buyers scramble for non-Middle East supply. Marathon Petroleum (NYSE: MPC) is similarly seen as a direct winner from the current environment, with refining margins climbing sharply as crude flows from the Persian Gulf face increasing uncertainty and disruption. LNG shortages are proving to be one of the most acute consequences of the conflict, as buyers across Europe and Asia move aggressively to secure alternative supply, driving spot prices to elevated levels not seen in recent years. Shipping costs have also reached extreme levels as tanker operators price in the heightened risk of operating near contested waterways, adding another layer of cost pressure throughout the global energy supply chain. The combination of higher crude prices, tightening LNG markets, record refining margins, and surging freight rates is creating a broad and sustained tailwind for energy companies with the right operational and geographic positioning to capture these multiple profit streams.
